title: P/E Ratio Explained: What Is a Good Price-to-Earnings Ratio?
summary: The P/E ratio explained in plain terms: how to calculate price-to-earnings, what a high or low P/E tells you, why there is no single good number, and when the ratio stops working.
body_markdown:
Investor.gov's[P/E ratio definition](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/price-earnings-pe-ratio) divides the current stock price by the current earnings per share, with EPS based on earnings for the past 12 months divided by the common shares outstanding. The SEC's[beginners' guide to financial statements](https://www.sec.gov/about/reports-publications/beginners-guide-financial-statements) gives the simplest example: a $20 share price and $2 of EPS is a P/E of 10, which means the stock sells for 10 times its earnings.


The EPS comes from the bottom of the[income statement](https://meetbenson.com/blog/how-to-read-an-income-statement/) . FINRA's[guide to financial performance metrics](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/financial-performance-metrics-every-investor-should-know) explains that companies usually report two figures there, basic and diluted EPS, and that diluted EPS is typically lower because it also counts the shares that would exist if convertible securities, stock options, and warrants were exercised. A lower EPS gives a higher P/E for the same price, so check which one a data site used before comparing two companies.
